newsitem.title: USA: No "witch-hunt" for chiefs' chairman - Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: No "witch-hunt" for chiefs' chairman - Pentagon.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen will not conduct a witch-hunt for sexual indiscretion in trying to assure that his choice to head the Joint Chiefs of Staff gains Senate approval, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.
Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston on Monday withdrew as a leading candidate to fill the top U.S. military post in an uproar over an adulterous affair that Ralston had 13 years ago and revealed last week.

Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters on Tuesday that Cohen will ask other top officers in the "vetting process" if there was anything he should know that would make them unacceptable or unable to lead the military.

But "the secretary is very much against witch-hunts. He has been from the beginning. He's applying a law, a rule of reason, to this entire search, as he has from the beginning," Bacon said in response to questions.
Cohen will not suggest a nominee to President Bill Clinton until after the secretary returns from a trip to Europe and the Gulf next week, the spokesman said.
Clinton has the final say on who will be nominated to the Senate for confirmation as the successor to the retiring JCS chairman, Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, on Sept. 30.
Bacon said Cohen was considering a number of top officers, including other members of the joint chiefs and commanders of U.S. forces around the world, to succeed Shalikashvili.

Ralston, 53, agreed to remain as vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff at least until his two-year term ends early in 1998 and Bacon again stressed Cohen's feeling that Ralston was qualified for the top job.
"What happened (to Ralston) was a public relations disaster," Bacon told reporters.
He said Ralston was caught in a mistaken perception that military justice was being applied unequally to men and women and junior and senior officers.

The news that Ralston was being considered for the top job despite a previous affair came after the Air Force forced Lt. Kelly Flinn, its first female bomber pilot, to resign to avoid a court-martial on adultery and other serious charges.
